issues.legal_issue: A legislature may impose a direct tax on buildings even when the tax base is measured by their value, without the levy becoming a tax on the total capital value of assets.
material_facts: The challenged law imposed a non-recurring tax directly on buildings.
It calculated the tax base by reference to a building’s annual value multiplied by a fixed factor.
The levy related to the building owned by the taxpayer rather than to the taxpayer’s total assets.
issues.conclusion: The State Legislature was competent to impose the building tax.
issues.legal_principle: Article 366(28) gives taxation a broad meaning. The distinction between the subject of a tax and the measure used to calculate its amount permits a direct tax on buildings under Entry 49 of List II, even if value is used as the measure; a tax on the total capital value of assets falls under Entry 86 of List I. The Court relied on Sudhir Chandra Nawn v. Wealth-Tax Officer and Assistant Commissioner of Urban Land Tax v. The Buckingham and Carnatic Co. Ltd.

predicates.tax_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenged the constitutional validity of a tax imposed on buildings.
predicates.levy_directly_attached_to_buildings: The legislature imposed the tax directly on buildings owned by taxpayers.
predicates.tax_base_measured_by_building_value: The tax amount was measured by the value of each building rather than by the taxpayer’s total assets.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a tax directly imposed on buildings and measured by their value, the rule treats the State Legislature as competent to impose that tax.

issues.legal_issue: A tax given effect from an earlier date is not invalid merely because it creates a tax liability for an earlier period if it does not impair an existing vested right or attach a new obligation to a completed transaction.
material_facts: The law was enacted after the date from which it imposed the building tax.
The taxpayers identified no vested right created by an existing law that the tax impaired.
The absence of an earlier building tax did not arise from a law granting a right to remain free from such taxation.
The levy did not attach a new obligation or disability to an earlier tax transaction or consideration.
issues.conclusion: The tax’s earlier effective date did not make the law retrospectively invalid in the strict technical sense.
issues.legal_principle: A statute is strictly retrospective if it takes away or impairs a vested right acquired under existing law, or creates a new obligation or disability in respect of a past transaction or consideration. The absence of an earlier taxing law does not itself create a vested right against a later levy. Where the enactment authorizes retrospective rates, the legislature may select the period. The Court relied on Bradford Union v. Wilts and The Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. The State of Bihar.

rule.if: retrospective_tax_challenge and tax_applies_to_past_period and no_vested_right_impairment and no_new_past_transaction_obligation

predicates.retrospective_tax_challenge: The proceeding challenged a tax law because it applied to a period before the law was enacted.
predicates.tax_applies_to_past_period: The legislature made the tax applicable to a period that preceded enactment.
predicates.no_vested_right_impairment: The challenger showed no vested right under existing law that the tax took away or impaired.
predicates.no_new_past_transaction_obligation: The tax attached no new obligation or disability to a transaction or consideration already past.

issues.definition: If a challenged tax applies to an earlier period but impairs no vested right and attaches no new obligation to a completed past transaction, its earlier effect does not make it invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature’s selection of an effective date for a tax classification does not violate equality merely because a different date could have been chosen, unless the selected date is arbitrary or unreasonably distant from a reasonable basis.
material_facts: The law imposed the tax from a date recommended during the legislative process.
The earlier law imposing a building tax had been invalidated, and the State later pursued a replacement measure.
The legislative history included a draft bill, consideration by a Select Committee, and ordinances preceding enactment.
The challengers did not show that the chosen date was capricious, whimsical, or wide of the reasonable mark.
issues.conclusion: The selected effective date was not discriminatory under Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: A date selected as a basis for classification is not arbitrary merely because no particular reason for that precise date is shown. It must be accepted unless it is capricious or whimsical, or is wide of the reasonable mark. The Court relied on Union of India v. M/s. Parameshwaran Match Works and referred to Louisville Gas Co. v. Alabama Power Co.

predicates.tax_date_classification_challenge: The proceeding challenged the effective date used to distinguish which buildings were subject to a tax.
predicates.date_selected_through_legislative_proces: The selected date emerged during legislative consideration and was followed by measures preceding enactment.
predicates.no_showing_date_is_unreasonable: The challengers did not establish that the selected date was capricious, whimsical, or outside a reasonable range.

issues.definition: When a challenged tax date emerged from legislative consideration and has not been shown to be unreasonable, the date-based classification is not discriminatory.

issues.legal_issue: A tax on buildings may include the ground on which a building stands and its integrated appurtenances without becoming a separate tax on land.
material_facts: The law defined a building to include a house or other structure.
A structure could not stand apart from the ground on which it was built, and that ground had no separate existence from the building for this purpose.
The law provided no separate method for assessing the annual or capital value of the ground as land.
The location and value of the land were considered as factors in determining the value of the building.
issues.conclusion: The tax was a tax on buildings, not a separate tax on land; the site and integrated appurtenances could be treated as components of the building.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 49 of List II permits a tax on lands, buildings, or both. The ordinary meaning of building includes its fabric, the ground on which its walls stand, and the ground within those walls. An appurtenance in its true sense is integrated with the building and has no independent existence for this purpose. The Court relied on Corporation of the City of Victoria v. Bishop of Vancouver Island and Maharaj Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and considered section 6(4) of the challenged law.

rule.if: tax_validity_challenge and tax_imposed_on_buildings and site_integral_to_structure and no_separate_land_assessment

predicates.tax_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenged the constitutional validity of a tax imposed on buildings.
predicates.tax_imposed_on_buildings: The legislature imposed the tax on buildings rather than assessing land as a separate taxable subject.
predicates.site_integral_to_structure: The ground beneath and within the structure was treated as integral to the building, and the appurtenance was integrated with its use.
predicates.no_separate_land_assessment: The law provided no separate method for assessing the ground as land apart from the building.

issues.definition: Where a tax is imposed on a building, its site is integral to the structure, and land is not separately assessed, the site and integrated appurtenances may be taxed as part of the building.

issues.legal_issue: A non-recurring building tax may use annual rental value and a uniform multiplier to estimate taxable capital value without being invalid merely because other valuation methods are available.
material_facts: The tax was non-recurring and therefore required a method of estimating value beyond annual taxation.
The law used annual value based on the rent a building could reasonably be expected to command and multiplied that value by a uniform factor.
The annual value was available through local authority records and could reflect the building’s rental capacity.
The challengers argued that the method and multiplier were hypothetical or arbitrary.
The Court found no single property valuation method to be perfect or immune from criticism.
issues.conclusion: Using annual value and the uniform multiplier to determine taxable capital value was not unconstitutional or legally infirm.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature may choose among reasonable methods for assessing tax, and a court will not substitute another method unless the chosen method is capricious, fanciful, arbitrary, or clearly unjust. Reasonable expected rent may be determined by accepted valuation methods, and there is no single legally mandatory method. The Court relied on Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income Tax Officer and discussed the valuation methods described in Faraday on Rating and State and Local Taxation by J. R. Hellerstein. It considered sections 2(a), 2(f), 5, and 6 of the challenged law.

rule.if: valuation_challenge_to_nonrecurring_building_tax and annual_rental_value_used_as_basis and uniform_multiplier_used and no_showing_method_is_arbitrary

predicates.valuation_challenge_to_nonrecurring_buil: The proceeding challenged the valuation formula for a non-recurring tax on buildings.
predicates.annual_rental_value_used_as_basis: The legislature used the rent a building could reasonably be expected to command as the basis for estimating its value.
predicates.uniform_multiplier_used: The legislature applied a uniform multiplier to annual value to estimate taxable capital value.
predicates.no_showing_method_is_arbitrary: The challengers did not establish that the selected valuation method was capricious, arbitrary, or clearly unjust.

issues.definition: When a non-recurring building tax uses reasonable expected annual rent and a uniform multiplier, and the method has not been shown to be arbitrary, the valuation formula is not invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A tax assessment law may rely on annual values fixed by local authorities without reproducing a separate valuation system if those authorities use a satisfactory statutory procedure and the tax law supplies adequate assessment machinery.
material_facts: The tax law adopted annual values recorded in local authority assessment books as the basis for determining building value.
The laws governing the relevant local authorities provided procedures for assessment, objections, appeals, and revisions.
The tax law provided procedures and machinery for assessing building tax on filed returns.
The challengers argued that the tax law itself lacked adequate machinery for determining annual value.
issues.conclusion: The assessment scheme was adequate and was not invalid for lack of procedural machinery.
issues.legal_principle: A taxing law may adopt a value fixed under another law where that value was determined through a satisfactory statutory procedure; a duplicate valuation system is unnecessary. The Court considered the procedures under the Kerala Municipal Corporation Act, 1961, the Kerala Municipalities Act, 1960, and the Kerala Panchayats Act, 1960, together with sections 9 to 16 of the challenged law.

rule.if: assessment_machinery_challenge and tax_law_uses_local_authority_values and local_value_set_by_satisfactory_procedure and tax_law_has_assessment_procedure

predicates.assessment_machinery_challenge: The proceeding challenged the adequacy of the procedures for assessing the tax.
predicates.tax_law_uses_local_authority_values: The tax law used annual values recorded in local authority assessment books.
predicates.local_value_set_by_satisfactory_procedur: The local authorities fixed annual values under statutory procedures providing assessment and avenues for objections, appeals, or revision.
predicates.tax_law_has_assessment_procedure: The tax law itself provided procedures for assessing the tax on returns filed by taxpayers.

issues.definition: If a tax law uses local values fixed through satisfactory statutory procedures and provides its own tax-assessment process, the assessment scheme is adequate.

issues.legal_issue: A uniform valuation formula does not treat buildings unequally where the underlying annual value reflects their differing capacity to command rent.
material_facts: The law determined annual value by the rent a building could reasonably be expected to command.
The law considered factors including the building’s location and the quality and nature of its construction.
Buildings in more desirable locations or with better construction and amenities could be expected to command higher rents.
The same multiplier was applied to annual values.
issues.conclusion: The uniform multiplier did not violate Article 14 by treating unequal buildings as equal.
issues.legal_principle: A common formula does not impermissibly treat unequal properties alike when the valuation input reflects relevant differences in their rental capacity. The Court applied Article 14 and considered the annual-value definition and section 6(4) of the challenged law.

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_building_valuation and annual_value_tracks_expected_rent and relevant_property_differences_affect_expected_rent and same_multiplier_applied

predicates.equality_challenge_to_building_valuation: The proceeding alleged that the building valuation formula discriminated between properties.
predicates.annual_value_tracks_expected_rent: The law assessed annual value by reference to the rent a building could reasonably be expected to command.
predicates.relevant_property_differences_affect_exp: Location, construction, or amenities affected the rent a building could reasonably be expected to command.
predicates.same_multiplier_applied: The law applied the same multiplier to the annual values of the buildings.

issues.definition: When annual value reflects relevant differences in expected rent, applying the same multiplier to those values does not make the formula discriminatory.

issues.legal_issue: The amount of a tax is generally a legislative matter and is not invalid merely because it is heavy unless the levy is confiscatory, extortionate, or a device for confiscating property.
material_facts: The challenged levy was a non-recurring tax on buildings calculated using a uniform multiplier.
The challengers argued that the resulting tax could exceed the construction cost of a building and could be disproportionate to competing investment returns.
The Court considered rental income, the non-recurring nature of the levy, and the potential appreciation in the building’s value.
The Court found no basis to characterize the levy as confiscatory or extortionate.
issues.conclusion: The tax’s amount and multiplier were not shown to be confiscatory, extortionate, or otherwise invalid.
issues.legal_principle: The quantum and conditions of a tax are within legislative competence; courts do not question the reasonableness of the amount unless the tax is confiscatory or extortionate. A taxing statute is not colourable merely because the levy is high; the legislature must be using taxation as a device or cloak for confiscation. The Court relied on Rai Ramkrishna v. State of Bihar, Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, Assistant Commissioner of Urban Land Tax v. The Buckingham and Carnatic Co. Ltd., Raja Jagannath Baksh Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and S. Kodar v. State of Kerala.

predicates.tax_amount_challenge: The proceeding challenged the amount or rate of the tax as unreasonable.
predicates.tax_is_nonrecurring: The tax was payable as a non-recurring charge on a building.
predicates.levy_not_shown_confiscatory_or_extortion: The challengers did not establish that the levy confiscated property or was extortionate.

issues.definition: A challenged tax amount is not invalid when the levy is non-recurring and has not been shown to be confiscatory or extortionate.

issues.legal_issue: A non-recurring building tax does not become extortionate because the tax is excluded from consideration when fair rent is fixed, where the tax is payable once and the rent-control law does not otherwise permit it to be considered.
material_facts: The law directed the rent-control court not to consider the building tax when fixing fair rent.
The building tax was a non-recurring liability payable by the owner.
The challengers identified no provision of the rent-control law under which the tax could otherwise have been considered in fixing fair rent.
The cases before the Court did not establish a concrete dispute in which the issue had arisen.
issues.conclusion: The exclusion of the tax from fair-rent calculations did not establish that the tax was extortionate or invalidate the provision.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed section 29 of the challenged law together with section 5 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965. It held that the one-time nature of the tax made apportionment to tenants over the tenancy period inapposite and that no rent-control provision had been identified as permitting the tax to be considered in fixing fair rent.

predicates.challenge_to_rent_pass_through: The proceeding challenged a rule preventing a building tax from being considered when fair rent was fixed.
predicates.owner_pays_tax_once: The owner incurred the building tax as a non-recurring liability.
predicates.rent_law_does_not_allow_tax_in_fair_rent: The governing rent law contained no identified provision permitting the tax to be included when fixing fair rent.

issues.definition: If the owner pays the tax once and the rent law does not allow it to be included in fair rent, excluding it from fair-rent calculations does not make the tax extortionate.

issues.legal_issue: An assessee who is entitled to pay a tax in instalments does not lose the right to appeal merely because the tax has not been paid in full, if the instalments have been paid as they fall due.
material_facts: The law permitted payment of the building tax in prescribed instalments.
The law also conditioned an appeal on payment of the tax due.
The Court considered how those provisions applied when an assessee paid each instalment as it became due.
issues.conclusion: An assessee who paid the instalments as they fell due was not barred from appealing for failure to pay the entire tax at once.
issues.legal_principle: The instalment provision and the appeal-payment condition must be read harmoniously. The Court construed sections 18 and 11(1) of the challenged law together.

predicates.tax_assessment_appeal: The proceeding concerned an appeal against a tax assessment or denial of liability.
predicates.tax_payable_in_installments: The law permitted the assessed tax to be paid in instalments.
predicates.assessee_paid_installments_as_due: The assessee paid each instalment when it fell due.

issues.definition: When an assessee appeals against a tax assessment, may pay in instalments, and has paid the instalments as they fall due, the appeal is not barred merely because future instalments remain unpaid.
